There have been a significant number of collisions where subsequent investigation has found that at some stage before impact, one or both parties were using VHF radio in an attempt to avoid collision.  The use of VHF radio in these circumstances is not always helpful and may even prove to be dangerous. 8.     At night, in restricted visibility or when there are more than two vessels in the vicinity, the need for positive identification is essential but this can rarely be guaranteed.  Uncertainties can arise over the identification of vessels and the interpretation of messages received. Even where positive identification has been achieved there is still the possibility of a misunderstanding due to language difficulties however fluent the parties concerned might be in the language being used.  An imprecise or ambiguously expressed message could have serious consequences. 9.  Valuable time can be wasted whilst mariners on vessels approaching each other try to make contact on VHF radio instead of complying with the Collision Regulations.  There is the further danger that even if contact and identification is achieved and no difficulties over the language of communication or message content arise, a course of action might still be chosen that does not comply with the Collision Regulations.  This may lead to the collision it was intended to prevent. 10.  In 1995, the judge in a collision case said "It is very probable that the use of VHF radio for conversation between these ships was a contributory cause of this collision, if only because it distracted the officers on watch from paying careful attention to their radar.  I must repeat, in the hope that it will achieve some publicity, what I have said on previous occasions that any attempt to use VHF to agree the manner of passing is fraught with the danger of misunderstanding.  Marine Superintendents would be well advised to prohibit such use of VHF radio and to instruct their officers to comply with the Collision Regulations." 11.  In a case published in 2002 one of two vessels, approaching each other in fog, used the VHF radio to call for a red to red (port to port) passing. The call was acknowledged by the other vessel but unfortunately, due to the command of English on the calling vessel, what the caller intended was a green to green (starboard to starboard) passing. The actions were not effectively monitored by either of the vessels and collision followed. 12. Again in a case published in 2006 one of two vessels, approaching one another to involve a close quarter’s situation, agreed to a starboard to starboard passing arrangement with a person on board another, unidentified ship, but not the approaching vessel. Furthermore, the passing agreement required one of the vessels to make an alteration of course, contrary to the requirements of the applicable Rule in the COLREGS. Had the vessel agreed to a passing arrangement requiring her to manoeuvre in compliance with the COLREGS, the ships would have passed clear, despite the misidentification of ships on the VHF radio. Unfortunately by the time both vessels realised that the ships had turned towards each other the distance between them had further reduced to the extent that the last minute avoiding action taken by both ships was unable to prevent a collision. 13. Numbers are also given their own standardized pronunciation on VHF radio to avoid confusion, particularly between numbers that sound alike when spoken quickly. Zero is pronounced ZERO. One is pronounced WUN. Two is pronounced TOO. Three is pronounced TREE. Four is pronounced FOWER. Five is pronounced FIFE. Six is pronounced SIX. Seven is pronounced SEVEN. Eight is pronounced AIT. Nine is pronounced NINER. Each digit of a multi-digit number, such as a call sign or a position, is read out individually rather than as a whole number, for example the number 79 is transmitted as SEVEN NINER, not as seventy-nine.

Why the Phonetic Alphabet Matters

Using the correct phonetic alphabet is not optional politeness, it is a regulatory requirement under the ITU Radio Regulations because misheard letters in a vessel name, call sign, or position can delay a search and rescue response or cause a message to be logged incorrectly by a coast station or Vessel Traffic Service. Before transmitting a spelled-out word, the operator should say "I SPELL" so the listening station knows individual letters are about to follow rather than a normal word, and should read the word back once at normal pace afterward so the listener can confirm they understood correctly.

7.   There have been a significant number of collisions where subsequent investigation has found that at some stage before impact, one or both parties were using VHF radio in an attempt to avoid collision.  The use of VHF radio in these circumstances is not always helpful and may even prove to be dangerous. 8.     At night, in restricted visibility or when there are more than two vessels in the vicinity, the need for positive identification is essential but this can rarely be guaranteed.  Uncertainties can arise over the identification of vessels and the interpretation of messages received. Even where positive identification has been achieved there is still the possibility of a misunderstanding due to language difficulties however fluent the parties concerned might be in the language being used.  An imprecise or ambiguously expressed message could have serious consequences. 9.  Valuable time can be wasted whilst mariners on vessels approaching each other try to make contact on VHF radio instead of complying with the Collision Regulations.  There is the further danger that even if contact and identification is achieved and no difficulties over the language of communication or message content arise, a course of action might still be chosen that does not comply with the Collision Regulations.  This may lead to the collision it was intended to prevent. 10.  In 1995, the judge in a collision case said "It is very probable that the use of VHF radio for conversation between these ships was a contributory cause of this collision, if only because it distracted the officers on watch from paying careful attention to their radar.  I must repeat, in the hope that it will achieve some publicity, what I have said on previous occasions that any attempt to use VHF to agree the manner of passing is fraught with the danger of misunderstanding.  Marine Superintendents would be well advised to prohibit such use of VHF radio and to instruct their officers to comply with the Collision Regulations." 11.  In a case published in 2002 one of two vessels, approaching each other in fog, used the VHF radio to call for a red to red (port to port) passing. The call was acknowledged by the other vessel but unfortunately, due to the command of English on the calling vessel, what the caller intended was a green to green (starboard to starboard) passing. The actions were not effectively monitored by either of the vessels and collision followed. 12. Again in a case published in 2006 one of two vessels, approaching one another to involve a close quarter’s situation, agreed to a starboard to starboard passing arrangement with a person on board another, unidentified ship, but not the approaching vessel. Furthermore, the passing agreement required one of the vessels to make an alteration of course, contrary to the requirements of the applicable Rule in the COLREGS. Had the vessel agreed to a passing arrangement requiring her to manoeuvre in compliance with the COLREGS, the ships would have passed clear, despite the misidentification of ships on the VHF radio. Unfortunately by the time both vessels realised that the ships had turned towards each other the distance between them had further reduced to the extent that the last minute avoiding action taken by both ships was unable to prevent a collision. 13.   Although the practice of using VHF radio as a collision avoidance aid may be resorted to on occasion, for example in pilotage waters, the risks described in this note should be clearly understood and the Collision Regulations complied with. - 3 -

[Excerpt 3 — VHFIMOSummaries.txt / Further Reading — Summaries]
**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mgn-324-mf-amendment-2-navigation-watchkeeping-safety-use-of-very-high-frequency-vhf-radio-and-automatic-identification-system-ais

MGN 324 (M+F) is MCA guidance directed at owners, masters, officers, and pilots of merchant ships, nautical training institutions, and owners/skippers of fishing vessels, yachts, and pleasure craft. It has been reissued and amended several times (the current version is "Amendment 2"), each time in response to continuing marine casualties in which misuse of VHF radio was identified as a contributory factor.

Its central message is that although VHF radio can be a useful aid to avoiding collisions, it must never be allowed to override or substitute for compliance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (COLREG) — in other words, a VHF conversation agreeing on a course of action between two vessels does not override the formal collision-avoidance rules, and over-reliance on VHF negotiation to resolve close-quarters situations has itself been a cause of accidents. The Note reiterates that marine VHF equipment must be used strictly in accordance with the ITU Radio Regulations described above.

The guidance also addresses the Automatic Identification System (AIS), clarifying that although AIS is not explicitly referenced in COLREG, it can usefully improve situational awareness for identifying ships, tracking targets, and gathering additional information. It cautions watchkeepers, however, that not all vessels carry AIS (particularly small leisure craft, fishing vessels, warships, and some shore stations), and that AIS may in some circumstances be legitimately switched off at a master's discretion — so officers of the watch should not treat the AIS picture as a complete or fully reliable representation of surrounding traffic. Taken together, the Note positions VHF and AIS as supplementary situational-awareness tools that must be used within, not instead of, the established rules and procedures for safe navigation.

- Traffic participants must indicate in good time if they wish to deviate from a route.
- During navigation assistance, the traffic controller gives an overview of the current traffic picture, possibly supplemented with calculated, expected situations, such as encounters and passages in (passing) distance and time.
- To convey the position of a moving ship, the position of the bow of the vessel relative to a point ahead in the fairway, or in bearing and distance, is used. For a stationary ship, this is the middle of the track or a radar echo.
- The **passing distance** is the distance that will exist during passing between the adjacent sides of two ships, or between a ship and an obstacle. The passing distance is only reliable provided the ground track remains constant.
- The **ground track** of a ship is its direction of movement relative to true north over the ground.
- The **distance between two vessels** is the measured shortest distance. For head-on traffic this is the bow-to-bow distance; for overtaking traffic this is the bow-to-stern distance.
- The **abeam distance** to a buoy, beacon or obstacle is the distance between the bow of a moving ship and an object, measured perpendicular to the direction of the fairway.
- The **distance to a navigation mark** is the shortest distance to that navigation mark.
- The terms **"opvarend" (upbound)** and **"afvarend" (downbound)** are used east of the Schone Waardin. In English these are "ingoing" and "outgoing".
- In the approach areas and the roadstead area, the terms **"inkomend" (inbound)** and **"uitgaand" (outbound)** are used, in English "inbound" and "outbound".
- To indicate a position before or beyond a certain point, we use **"bovenwaarts" (upstream)** or **"benedenwaarts" (downstream)**. In English these are "above" and "below".
- If the traffic controller must give information about a part of the area not covered by radar and for which no visual information is available, he or she will make this known to the traffic participant requesting the information.
- Position information is always given relative to known reference points. These points are visible, known and can be found on the nautical chart.
- A **bearing** between two known points is the horizontal angle relative to true north and the point being observed. The figures are spoken one by one.
- **Distances** are given to a tenth of a kilometre or a tenth of a nautical mile (also called a "cable"). Where confusion is possible, e.g. between the English numbers fifty and fifteen, the digits are spoken separately.
- Names of buoys and markers must not be translated. They are pronounced as they appear on the nautical chart. For example, W6 is pronounced "Whiskey 6".
- "Buoy transit" (doorwisselen van boeien) refers to two consecutive buoys marking a bend in a channel coming into line relative to the bow of the ship.
- Position reports can be given in two ways: using the along/across method, or via bearing and distance. The traffic controller may supplement this with ground track and ground speed. The intervals between reports depend on the traffic picture, the speeds of vessels, meteorological conditions, nautically critical points, and so on.
- An **along/across position report** comprises, on the one hand, the point to which the ship has progressed along the length of the fairway, and on the other hand, the distance of the ship in the transverse direction, measured to the locally customary reference line — for example the buoy line, the light line, the shore, etc. The transverse distance may also be expressed as 1/3 red, 1/3 green, or mid-channel. If the distance is less than 1/3 of the fairway width, the distance is expressed in metres to the buoy line.
  Measurements are always given relative to the starboard side (SB) of the vessel. If this is not possible because there is no reference, the traffic controller will explicitly state this.
- A **position report via bearing and distance** looks at the position of the forward part of the assisted ship in relation to a known point.
  Here too, the traffic controller may add ground track and ground speed. If the ship is sailing parallel to the reference line, moving away from it, or approaching it, this will be stated.
- If the traffic controller gives position reports (on request) while a ship is coming to anchor, he or she agrees which point the reports will be relative to. Either the planned anchor position is indicated — this may be an anchorage as shown on the chart, or a position chosen by the master or pilot. From the bow, the traffic controller gives information by bearing and distance (B/D) to the anchor position, including speed over ground. As a standard for reporting frequency, the following applies:
  - Distance more than 1500 m: B/D every 500 m
  - Distance 1500 to 500 m: B/D every 200 m
  - Distance 500 to 200 m: B/D every 100 m
  - From 200 m: B/D every 50 m.

For anchor watch purposes, the master or pilot must state the number of nautical miles and/or cables relative to a fixed point, and the number of shackles on deck.

MGN 324 (M+F) is MCA guidance directed at owners, masters, officers, and pilots of merchant ships, nautical training institutions, and owners/skippers of fishing vessels, yachts, and pleasure craft. It has been reissued and amended several times (the current version is "Amendment 2"), each time in response to continuing marine casualties in which misuse of VHF radio was identified as a contributory factor.

Its central message is that although VHF radio can be a useful aid to avoiding collisions, it must never be allowed to override or substitute for compliance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (COLREG) — in other words, a VHF conversation agreeing on a course of action between two vessels does not override the formal collision-avoidance rules, and over-reliance on VHF negotiation to resolve close-quarters situations has itself been a cause of accidents. The Note reiterates that marine VHF equipment must be used strictly in accordance with the ITU Radio Regulations described above.

The guidance also addresses the Automatic Identification System (AIS), clarifying that although AIS is not explicitly referenced in COLREG, it can usefully improve situational awareness for identifying ships, tracking targets, and gathering additional information. It cautions watchkeepers, however, that not all vessels carry AIS (particularly small leisure craft, fishing vessels, warships, and some shore stations), and that AIS may in some circumstances be legitimately switched off at a master's discretion — so officers of the watch should not treat the AIS picture as a complete or fully reliable representation of surrounding traffic. Taken together, the Note positions VHF and AIS as supplementary situational-awareness tools that must be used within, not instead of, the established rules and procedures for safe navigation.

Rule No. 1: Respect the channel designations, especially those of the "big three." Channel 16 is reserved for distress and safety calls and for contact calls to other vessels or shore stations. Channel 13 is used for vessel bridge-to-bridge communications and is heavily trafficked by commercial ships for intership navigation. And Channel 22A is used for safety broadcasts and U.S. Coast Guard communications; after hailing on 16, you're usually asked to switch to 22A. Because of congestion on 16, Channel 9 has been designated as an alternate contact-calling channel between pleasure vessels and to shore stations but, except in some areas, the Coast Guard doesn't transmit safety messages on 9. You should always monitor 16 in case a nearby boat needs help and to hear Coast Guard safety messages. Ideally, it's good to have two VHFs, one set on 9 and another tuned to 16.

Do regular radio checks, but the U.S. Coast Guard requests that you do so on Channel 09, which has been designated as a boater’s calling channel by FCC. Something the authorities find quite aggravating is when a recreational boater requests a "radio check" on Channel 16 (an emergency channel. Hailing "TowBoatUS" on 68 is an easy way to conduct a check.

What channels should you use for regular conversations? Channels 68, 69, 71, 72, and 78A are considered non-commercial channels, and in most areas, 68 and 72 are commonly used by the recreational-boating community. But remember that the VHF is officially for "operational" purposes. This can be as informal as passing on a weather report, but conversations about what the dog chewed up yesterday are inappropriate. Some channels, such as 70, have restricted use, and you can't use them for voice communications.

Whatever type of conversation you may be having, remember that no one else within a 20-mile range can talk on that channel while you're talking. Considering the limited number of appropriate channels, an extended conversation can inconvenience a large number of other boaters. So keep your VHF communications brief and to the point. If you're communicating with a boat that's close by (within a mile or two), you should switch over to low power. Both fixed-mount and handheld VHFs have low-power settings, which limit the range of your broadcast and thereby limit the number of other boaters you may be blocking out due to your transmission.

Remember that everyone can hear you. It's very easy to offend a large number of people on the VHF, and there are often small children listening.

There have been a significant number of collisions where subsequent investigation has found that at some stage before impact, one or both parties were using VHF radio in an attempt to avoid collision.  The use of VHF radio in these circumstances is not always helpful and may even prove to be dangerous. 8.     At night, in restricted visibility or when there are more than two vessels in the vicinity, the need for positive identification is essential but this can rarely be guaranteed.  Uncertainties can arise over the identification of vessels and the interpretation of messages received. Even where positive identification has been achieved there is still the possibility of a misunderstanding due to language difficulties however fluent the parties concerned might be in the language being used.  An imprecise or ambiguously expressed message could have serious consequences. 9.  Valuable time can be wasted whilst mariners on vessels approaching each other try to make contact on VHF radio instead of complying with the Collision Regulations.  There is the further danger that even if contact and identification is achieved and no difficulties over the language of communication or message content arise, a course of action might still be chosen that does not comply with the Collision Regulations.  This may lead to the collision it was intended to prevent. 10.  In 1995, the judge in a collision case said "It is very probable that the use of VHF radio for conversation between these ships was a contributory cause of this collision, if only because it distracted the officers on watch from paying careful attention to their radar.  I must repeat, in the hope that it will achieve some publicity, what I have said on previous occasions that any attempt to use VHF to agree the manner of passing is fraught with the danger of misunderstanding.  Marine Superintendents would be well advised to prohibit such use of VHF radio and to instruct their officers to comply with the Collision Regulations." 11.  In a case published in 2002 one of two vessels, approaching each other in fog, used the VHF radio to call for a red to red (port to port) passing. The call was acknowledged by the other vessel but unfortunately, due to the command of English on the calling vessel, what the caller intended was a green to green (starboard to starboard) passing. The actions were not effectively monitored by either of the vessels and collision followed. 12. Again in a case published in 2006 one of two vessels, approaching one another to involve a close quarter’s situation, agreed to a starboard to starboard passing arrangement with a person on board another, unidentified ship, but not the approaching vessel. MGN 641 (M) is the MCA's practical guidance document explaining how shipowners, masters, shipbuilders, and seafarers should interpret and apply the Merchant Shipping (Radiocommunications) (Amendment) Regulations 2021 described above. Rather than creating new legal obligations itself, it is meant to be read alongside the 2021 Regulations to clarify what compliance looks like in practice — and in fact parts of the Note have been given the force of law by the Regulations.

The guidance is structured around eight key topic areas: an introduction to the legal framework; how "recognised satellite service providers" are determined; requirements for radio installation on board; the sources of electrical energy that must be available to power radio equipment (including backup power in case of failure); the performance standards equipment must meet; maintenance requirements to keep radio equipment serviceable; qualifications and duties required of radio personnel on board; and the record-keeping obligations for radio logs.

Because the Regulations incorporate future SOLAS amendments automatically via the ambulatory reference mechanism, the guidance note is periodically reissued or amended (there have been at least one or two amendments since first publication in December 2021) to reflect the latest position and remove ambiguity for those applying the rules day to day.

[Excerpt 2 — VHF-procedures-Scheldt-area-EN.md / VHF PROCEDURES]
- Traffic participants must indicate in good time if they wish to deviate from a route.
- During navigation assistance, the traffic controller gives an overview of the current traffic picture, possibly supplemented with calculated, expected situations, such as encounters and passages in (passing) distance and time.
- To convey the position of a moving ship, the position of the bow of the vessel relative to a point ahead in the fairway, or in bearing and distance, is used. For a stationary ship, this is the middle of the track or a radar echo.
- The **passing distance** is the distance that will exist during passing between the adjacent sides of two ships, or between a ship and an obstacle. The passing distance is only reliable provided the ground track remains constant.
- The **ground track** of a ship is its direction of movement relative to true north over the ground.
- The **distance between two vessels** is the measured shortest distance. For head-on traffic this is the bow-to-bow distance; for overtaking traffic this is the bow-to-stern distance.
- The **abeam distance** to a buoy, beacon or obstacle is the distance between the bow of a moving ship and an object, measured perpendicular to the direction of the fairway.
- The **distance to a navigation mark** is the shortest distance to that navigation mark.
- The terms **"opvarend" (upbound)** and **"afvarend" (downbound)** are used east of the Schone Waardin. In English these are "ingoing" and "outgoing".
- In the approach areas and the roadstead area, the terms **"inkomend" (inbound)** and **"uitgaand" (outbound)** are used, in English "inbound" and "outbound".
- To indicate a position before or beyond a certain point, we use **"bovenwaarts" (upstream)** or **"benedenwaarts" (downstream)**. In English these are "above" and "below".
- If the traffic controller must give information about a part of the area not covered by radar and for which no visual information is available, he or she will make this known to the traffic participant requesting the information.
- Position information is always given relative to known reference points. These points are visible, known and can be found on the nautical chart.
- A **bearing** between two known points is the horizontal angle relative to true north and the point being observed. The figures are spoken one by one.
- **Distances** are given to a tenth of a kilometre or a tenth of a nautical mile (also called a "cable"). Where confusion is possible, e.g. between the English numbers fifty and fifteen, the digits are spoken separately.
- Names of buoys and markers must not be translated. They are pronounced as they appear on the nautical chart. For example, W6 is pronounced "Whiskey 6".
- "Buoy transit" (doorwisselen van boeien) refers to two consecutive buoys marking a bend in a channel coming into line relative to the bow of the ship.
- Position reports can be given in two ways: using the along/across method, or via bearing and distance. The traffic controller may supplement this with ground track and ground speed. The intervals between reports depend on the traffic picture, the speeds of vessels, meteorological conditions, nautically critical points, and so on.
- An **along/across position report** comprises, on the one hand, the point to which the ship has progressed along the length of the fairway, and on the other hand, the distance of the ship in the transverse direction, measured to the locally customary reference line — for example the buoy line, the light line, the shore, etc. The transverse distance may also be expressed as 1/3 red, 1/3 green, or mid-channel. If the distance is less than 1/3 of the fairway width, the distance is expressed in metres to the buoy line.
  Measurements are always given relative to the starboard side (SB) of the vessel. If this is not possible because there is no reference, the traffic controller will explicitly state this.
- A **position report via bearing and distance** looks at the position of the forward part of the assisted ship in relation to a known point.
  Here too, the traffic controller may add ground track and ground speed. If the ship is sailing parallel to the reference line, moving away from it, or approaching it, this will be stated.
- If the traffic controller gives position reports (on request) while a ship is coming to anchor, he or she agrees which point the reports will be relative to. Either the planned anchor position is indicated — this may be an anchorage as shown on the chart, or a position chosen by the master or pilot. From the bow, the traffic controller gives information by bearing and distance (B/D) to the anchor position, including speed over ground. As a standard for reporting frequency, the following applies:
  - Distance more than 1500 m: B/D every 500 m
  - Distance 1500 to 500 m: B/D every 200 m
  - Distance 500 to 200 m: B/D every 100 m
  - From 200 m: B/D every 50 m.

For anchor watch purposes, the master or pilot must state the number of nautical miles and/or cables relative to a fixed point, and the number of shackles on deck.

[Excerpt 3 — VHF-procedures-Scheldt-area-EN.md / VHF PROCEDURES]
The waterway user indicates when navigation assistance should be started and stopped by reporting in and out on the radar channel. The term **"navigation assistance"** is always used for this.¹

A traffic controller may also initiate the use of (elements of) navigation assistance on their own initiative in the event of deviant sailing behaviour.

- The traffic controller will confirm that the ship wants navigation assistance.
- In addition, the traffic controller will ask seagoing vessels in particular whether "buoy transits" (doorwisselen van boeien) are also desired.
  - Answer no: the traffic controller does not include the reporting of buoy transits as standard in the report.
  - Answer yes: the traffic controller includes the report of buoy transits (in a bend or during major course changes) as standard in the report.
- The waterway user then receives an initial message containing the following elements:
  - Understood/Acknowledged.
  - The own position of the ship that reported in for navigation assistance, according to the along/across method or the Bearing and Distance method (B/D method).
  - A relevant traffic picture of the ships in the vicinity.
- The traffic controller will also provide updates with the following content:
  - Own position of the ship according to the along/across or B/D method.
  - The aim is to provide this at least at every buoy or every second buoy, according to the traffic controller's assessment.

**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mgn-324-mf-amendment-2-navigation-watchkeeping-safety-use-of-very-high-frequency-vhf-radio-and-automatic-identification-system-ais

MGN 324 (M+F) is MCA guidance directed at owners, masters, officers, and pilots of merchant ships, nautical training institutions, and owners/skippers of fishing vessels, yachts, and pleasure craft. It has been reissued and amended several times (the current version is "Amendment 2"), each time in response to continuing marine casualties in which misuse of VHF radio was identified as a contributory factor.

Its central message is that although VHF radio can be a useful aid to avoiding collisions, it must never be allowed to override or substitute for compliance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (COLREG) — in other words, a VHF conversation agreeing on a course of action between two vessels does not override the formal collision-avoidance rules, and over-reliance on VHF negotiation to resolve close-quarters situations has itself been a cause of accidents. The Note reiterates that marine VHF equipment must be used strictly in accordance with the ITU Radio Regulations described above.

The guidance also addresses the Automatic Identification System (AIS), clarifying that although AIS is not explicitly referenced in COLREG, it can usefully improve situational awareness for identifying ships, tracking targets, and gathering additional information. It cautions watchkeepers, however, that not all vessels carry AIS (particularly small leisure craft, fishing vessels, warships, and some shore stations), and that AIS may in some circumstances be legitimately switched off at a master's discretion — so officers of the watch should not treat the AIS picture as a complete or fully reliable representation of surrounding traffic. Taken together, the Note positions VHF and AIS as supplementary situational-awareness tools that must be used within, not instead of, the established rules and procedures for safe navigation.

If users of VHF channels do not observe communication discipline, cross-talk occurs. This cross-talk, also known as interference, disrupts normal message traffic and creates questions that do not benefit safety. To prevent interference on the VHF channels, VHF users must observe the following rules:

- All conversations over VHF must be short, businesslike and clear, and take place on the correct channel (communication discipline).
- All VHF installations must transmit at a power of no more than 1 watt.
- Within VTS-SG, a reporting obligation and listening-watch obligation applies to all commercial shipping.
- For recreational craft with a VHF installation on board, a duty to be reachable applies, but not a reporting obligation (see the folder *VHF Sectors in the Scheldt Area*).
- Monitoring the traffic channel is mandatory at all times. In case of congestion or other circumstances, a radar channel can serve as an overflow.
- If a traffic controller foresees bottlenecks or dangerous situations, he or she actively intervenes to prevent problems. The traffic controller uses his or her authority to give a warning, information, advice or a traffic instruction.
- Without prejudice to the powers of the Flemish and Dutch authorities, and in the context of the safe and smooth handling of shipping traffic, ultimate responsibility for navigation always rests with the master/traffic participant.
- Traffic arrangements between ships, such as passing or overtaking not in accordance with the applicable navigation rules, are made directly between the ships themselves. When crossing, reference is usually made to the colour of the sidelights, for example: "We are passing green to green." When overtaking, reference is usually made to the side, for example: "I am passing on the port/starboard side." This is the traffic-regulating character of such arrangements.
- All traffic participants and traffic controllers must comply with these prescribed VHF procedures.

[Excerpt 2 — VHF-procedures-Scheldt-area-EN.md / VHF PROCEDURES]
- Traffic participants must indicate in good time if they wish to deviate from a route.
- During navigation assistance, the traffic controller gives an overview of the current traffic picture, possibly supplemented with calculated, expected situations, such as encounters and passages in (passing) distance and time.
- To convey the position of a moving ship, the position of the bow of the vessel relative to a point ahead in the fairway, or in bearing and distance, is used. For a stationary ship, this is the middle of the track or a radar echo.
- The **passing distance** is the distance that will exist during passing between the adjacent sides of two ships, or between a ship and an obstacle. The passing distance is only reliable provided the ground track remains constant.
- The **ground track** of a ship is its direction of movement relative to true north over the ground.
- The **distance between two vessels** is the measured shortest distance. For head-on traffic this is the bow-to-bow distance; for overtaking traffic this is the bow-to-stern distance.
- The **abeam distance** to a buoy, beacon or obstacle is the distance between the bow of a moving ship and an object, measured perpendicular to the direction of the fairway.
- The **distance to a navigation mark** is the shortest distance to that navigation mark.
- The terms **"opvarend" (upbound)** and **"afvarend" (downbound)** are used east of the Schone Waardin. In English these are "ingoing" and "outgoing".
- In the approach areas and the roadstead area, the terms **"inkomend" (inbound)** and **"uitgaand" (outbound)** are used, in English "inbound" and "outbound".
- To indicate a position before or beyond a certain point, we use **"bovenwaarts" (upstream)** or **"benedenwaarts" (downstream)**. In English these are "above" and "below".
- If the traffic controller must give information about a part of the area not covered by radar and for which no visual information is available, he or she will make this known to the traffic participant requesting the information.
- Position information is always given relative to known reference points. These points are visible, known and can be found on the nautical chart.
- A **bearing** between two known points is the horizontal angle relative to true north and the point being observed. The figures are spoken one by one.
- **Distances** are given to a tenth of a kilometre or a tenth of a nautical mile (also called a "cable"). Where confusion is possible, e.g. between the English numbers fifty and fifteen, the digits are spoken separately.
- Names of buoys and markers must not be translated. They are pronounced as they appear on the nautical chart. For example, W6 is pronounced "Whiskey 6".
- "Buoy transit" (doorwisselen van boeien) refers to two consecutive buoys marking a bend in a channel coming into line relative to the bow of the ship.
- Position reports can be given in two ways: using the along/across method, or via bearing and distance. The traffic controller may supplement this with ground track and ground speed. The intervals between reports depend on the traffic picture, the speeds of vessels, meteorological conditions, nautically critical points, and so on.
- An **along/across position report** comprises, on the one hand, the point to which the ship has progressed along the length of the fairway, and on the other hand, the distance of the ship in the transverse direction, measured to the locally customary reference line — for example the buoy line, the light line, the shore, etc. The transverse distance may also be expressed as 1/3 red, 1/3 green, or mid-channel. If the distance is less than 1/3 of the fairway width, the distance is expressed in metres to the buoy line.
  Measurements are always given relative to the starboard side (SB) of the vessel. If this is not possible because there is no reference, the traffic controller will explicitly state this.
- A **position report via bearing and distance** looks at the position of the forward part of the assisted ship in relation to a known point.
  Here too, the traffic controller may add ground track and ground speed. If the ship is sailing parallel to the reference line, moving away from it, or approaching it, this will be stated.
- If the traffic controller gives position reports (on request) while a ship is coming to anchor, he or she agrees which point the reports will be relative to. Either the planned anchor position is indicated — this may be an anchorage as shown on the chart, or a position chosen by the master or pilot. From the bow, the traffic controller gives information by bearing and distance (B/D) to the anchor position, including speed over ground. As a standard for reporting frequency, the following applies:
  - Distance more than 1500 m: B/D every 500 m
  - Distance 1500 to 500 m: B/D every 200 m
  - Distance 500 to 200 m: B/D every 100 m
  - From 200 m: B/D every 50 m.

For anchor watch purposes, the master or pilot must state the number of nautical miles and/or cables relative to a fixed point, and the number of shackles on deck.

MGN 324 (M+F) is MCA guidance directed at owners, masters, officers, and pilots of merchant ships, nautical training institutions, and owners/skippers of fishing vessels, yachts, and pleasure craft. It has been reissued and amended several times (the current version is "Amendment 2"), each time in response to continuing marine casualties in which misuse of VHF radio was identified as a contributory factor.

Its central message is that although VHF radio can be a useful aid to avoiding collisions, it must never be allowed to override or substitute for compliance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (COLREG) — in other words, a VHF conversation agreeing on a course of action between two vessels does not override the formal collision-avoidance rules, and over-reliance on VHF negotiation to resolve close-quarters situations has itself been a cause of accidents. The Note reiterates that marine VHF equipment must be used strictly in accordance with the ITU Radio Regulations described above.

The guidance also addresses the Automatic Identification System (AIS), clarifying that although AIS is not explicitly referenced in COLREG, it can usefully improve situational awareness for identifying ships, tracking targets, and gathering additional information. It cautions watchkeepers, however, that not all vessels carry AIS (particularly small leisure craft, fishing vessels, warships, and some shore stations), and that AIS may in some circumstances be legitimately switched off at a master's discretion — so officers of the watch should not treat the AIS picture as a complete or fully reliable representation of surrounding traffic. Taken together, the Note positions VHF and AIS as supplementary situational-awareness tools that must be used within, not instead of, the established rules and procedures for safe navigation.

How to Hail Another Vessel or Marina in 2026?
Hailing is the process of making initial contact with another station. Doing it properly shows you understand radio etiquette and gets you a faster response. Many new boaters feel nervous about their first hails, but following a simple script makes the process straightforward.

The Standard Hailing Protocol
Start by tuning to Channel 16. Listen briefly to ensure the channel is not in use. Then press your PTT button and say the name of the station you are calling, followed by your own vessel name, then the word “over.” For example: “Marina Del Ray, Marina Del Ray, this is sailing vessel Windward, over.”

Wait 15 to 30 seconds for a response. If you do not hear anything, try again. If there is still no response after three attempts, the station may not be monitoring or may be out of range. MGN 324 (M+F) is MCA guidance directed at owners, masters, officers, and pilots of merchant ships, nautical training institutions, and owners/skippers of fishing vessels, yachts, and pleasure craft. It has been reissued and amended several times (the current version is "Amendment 2"), each time in response to continuing marine casualties in which misuse of VHF radio was identified as a contributory factor.

Its central message is that although VHF radio can be a useful aid to avoiding collisions, it must never be allowed to override or substitute for compliance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (COLREG) — in other words, a VHF conversation agreeing on a course of action between two vessels does not override the formal collision-avoidance rules, and over-reliance on VHF negotiation to resolve close-quarters situations has itself been a cause of accidents. The Note reiterates that marine VHF equipment must be used strictly in accordance with the ITU Radio Regulations described above.

The guidance also addresses the Automatic Identification System (AIS), clarifying that although AIS is not explicitly referenced in COLREG, it can usefully improve situational awareness for identifying ships, tracking targets, and gathering additional information. It cautions watchkeepers, however, that not all vessels carry AIS (particularly small leisure craft, fishing vessels, warships, and some shore stations), and that AIS may in some circumstances be legitimately switched off at a master's discretion — so officers of the watch should not treat the AIS picture as a complete or fully reliable representation of surrounding traffic. Taken together, the Note positions VHF and AIS as supplementary situational-awareness tools that must be used within, not instead of, the established rules and procedures for safe navigation.

If users of VHF channels do not observe communication discipline, cross-talk occurs. This cross-talk, also known as interference, disrupts normal message traffic and creates questions that do not benefit safety. To prevent interference on the VHF channels, VHF users must observe the following rules:

- All conversations over VHF must be short, businesslike and clear, and take place on the correct channel (communication discipline).
- All VHF installations must transmit at a power of no more than 1 watt.
- Within VTS-SG, a reporting obligation and listening-watch obligation applies to all commercial shipping.
- For recreational craft with a VHF installation on board, a duty to be reachable applies, but not a reporting obligation (see the folder *VHF Sectors in the Scheldt Area*).
- Monitoring the traffic channel is mandatory at all times. In case of congestion or other circumstances, a radar channel can serve as an overflow.
- If a traffic controller foresees bottlenecks or dangerous situations, he or she actively intervenes to prevent problems. The traffic controller uses his or her authority to give a warning, information, advice or a traffic instruction.
- Without prejudice to the powers of the Flemish and Dutch authorities, and in the context of the safe and smooth handling of shipping traffic, ultimate responsibility for navigation always rests with the master/traffic participant.
- Traffic arrangements between ships, such as passing or overtaking not in accordance with the applicable navigation rules, are made directly between the ships themselves. When crossing, reference is usually made to the colour of the sidelights, for example: "We are passing green to green." When overtaking, reference is usually made to the side, for example: "I am passing on the port/starboard side." This is the traffic-regulating character of such arrangements.
- All traffic participants and traffic controllers must comply with these prescribed VHF procedures.

[Excerpt 2 — VHF-procedures-Scheldt-area-EN.md / VHF PROCEDURES]
- Traffic participants must indicate in good time if they wish to deviate from a route.
- During navigation assistance, the traffic controller gives an overview of the current traffic picture, possibly supplemented with calculated, expected situations, such as encounters and passages in (passing) distance and time.
- To convey the position of a moving ship, the position of the bow of the vessel relative to a point ahead in the fairway, or in bearing and distance, is used. For a stationary ship, this is the middle of the track or a radar echo.
- The **passing distance** is the distance that will exist during passing between the adjacent sides of two ships, or between a ship and an obstacle. The passing distance is only reliable provided the ground track remains constant.
- The **ground track** of a ship is its direction of movement relative to true north over the ground.
- The **distance between two vessels** is the measured shortest distance. For head-on traffic this is the bow-to-bow distance; for overtaking traffic this is the bow-to-stern distance.
- The **abeam distance** to a buoy, beacon or obstacle is the distance between the bow of a moving ship and an object, measured perpendicular to the direction of the fairway.
- The **distance to a navigation mark** is the shortest distance to that navigation mark.
- The terms **"opvarend" (upbound)** and **"afvarend" (downbound)** are used east of the Schone Waardin. In English these are "ingoing" and "outgoing".
- In the approach areas and the roadstead area, the terms **"inkomend" (inbound)** and **"uitgaand" (outbound)** are used, in English "inbound" and "outbound".
- To indicate a position before or beyond a certain point, we use **"bovenwaarts" (upstream)** or **"benedenwaarts" (downstream)**. In English these are "above" and "below".
- If the traffic controller must give information about a part of the area not covered by radar and for which no visual information is available, he or she will make this known to the traffic participant requesting the information.
- Position information is always given relative to known reference points. These points are visible, known and can be found on the nautical chart.
- A **bearing** between two known points is the horizontal angle relative to true north and the point being observed. The figures are spoken one by one.
- **Distances** are given to a tenth of a kilometre or a tenth of a nautical mile (also called a "cable"). Where confusion is possible, e.g. between the English numbers fifty and fifteen, the digits are spoken separately.
- Names of buoys and markers must not be translated. They are pronounced as they appear on the nautical chart. For example, W6 is pronounced "Whiskey 6".
- "Buoy transit" (doorwisselen van boeien) refers to two consecutive buoys marking a bend in a channel coming into line relative to the bow of the ship.
- Position reports can be given in two ways: using the along/across method, or via bearing and distance. The traffic controller may supplement this with ground track and ground speed. The intervals between reports depend on the traffic picture, the speeds of vessels, meteorological conditions, nautically critical points, and so on.
- An **along/across position report** comprises, on the one hand, the point to which the ship has progressed along the length of the fairway, and on the other hand, the distance of the ship in the transverse direction, measured to the locally customary reference line — for example the buoy line, the light line, the shore, etc. The transverse distance may also be expressed as 1/3 red, 1/3 green, or mid-channel. If the distance is less than 1/3 of the fairway width, the distance is expressed in metres to the buoy line.
  Measurements are always given relative to the starboard side (SB) of the vessel. If this is not possible because there is no reference, the traffic controller will explicitly state this.
- A **position report via bearing and distance** looks at the position of the forward part of the assisted ship in relation to a known point.
  Here too, the traffic controller may add ground track and ground speed. If the ship is sailing parallel to the reference line, moving away from it, or approaching it, this will be stated.
- If the traffic controller gives position reports (on request) while a ship is coming to anchor, he or she agrees which point the reports will be relative to. Either the planned anchor position is indicated — this may be an anchorage as shown on the chart, or a position chosen by the master or pilot. From the bow, the traffic controller gives information by bearing and distance (B/D) to the anchor position, including speed over ground. As a standard for reporting frequency, the following applies:
  - Distance more than 1500 m: B/D every 500 m
  - Distance 1500 to 500 m: B/D every 200 m
  - Distance 500 to 200 m: B/D every 100 m
  - From 200 m: B/D every 50 m.

For anchor watch purposes, the master or pilot must state the number of nautical miles and/or cables relative to a fixed point, and the number of shackles on deck.

A Vessel Traffic Service is a service implemented by the authorities that provides the means to communicate with shipping traffic and to respond to situations developing within the VTS area. The service increases the safety and efficiency of shipping and contributes to "Safety of Life at Sea" and to environmental protection.

A VTS is responsible for:

- **Providing timely and relevant information** about factors that may influence navigation and that support the on-board decision-making process.
  This includes, among other things, information on the position, identity and destination of other ships, and hydrological and meteorological information.

- **Monitoring and planning vessels** so as to contribute to the safe and smooth handling of shipping traffic.
  This involves providing essential, up-to-date and timely information to support the on-board navigational decision-making process. This support consists of providing timely information, advice and instructions. The information may relate to anything in the chain of operations, such as lock planning, tidal windows, the availability of pilotage services, and so on.

- **Providing timely and relevant information** to respond to the development of unsafe situations.
  Essential, up-to-date and timely information is provided to support the on-board navigational decision-making process. This support consists of providing timely information, advice and traffic instructions.

A Vessel Traffic Service is a service implemented by the authorities that provides the means to communicate with shipping traffic and to respond to situations developing within the VTS area. The service increases the safety and efficiency of shipping and contributes to "Safety of Life at Sea" and to environmental protection.

A VTS is responsible for:

- **Providing timely and relevant information** about factors that may influence navigation and that support the on-board decision-making process.
  This includes, among other things, information on the position, identity and destination of other ships, and hydrological and meteorological information.

- **Monitoring and planning vessels** so as to contribute to the safe and smooth handling of shipping traffic.
  This involves providing essential, up-to-date and timely information to support the on-board navigational decision-making process. This support consists of providing timely information, advice and instructions. The information may relate to anything in the chain of operations, such as lock planning, tidal windows, the availability of pilotage services, and so on.

- **Providing timely and relevant information** to respond to the development of unsafe situations.
  Essential, up-to-date and timely information is provided to support the on-board navigational decision-making process. This support consists of providing timely information, advice and traffic instructions.

To achieve this, a VTS can provide information, warnings or traffic instructions where necessary.

[Excerpt 3 — VHFIMOSummaries.txt / Further Reading — Summaries]
**Link:** https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mgn-324-mf-amendment-2-navigation-watchkeeping-safety-use-of-very-high-frequency-vhf-radio-and-automatic-identification-system-ais

MGN 324 (M+F) is MCA guidance directed at owners, masters, officers, and pilots of merchant ships, nautical training institutions, and owners/skippers of fishing vessels, yachts, and pleasure craft. It has been reissued and amended several times (the current version is "Amendment 2"), each time in response to continuing marine casualties in which misuse of VHF radio was identified as a contributory factor.

Its central message is that although VHF radio can be a useful aid to avoiding collisions, it must never be allowed to override or substitute for compliance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (COLREG) — in other words, a VHF conversation agreeing on a course of action between two vessels does not override the formal collision-avoidance rules, and over-reliance on VHF negotiation to resolve close-quarters situations has itself been a cause of accidents. The Note reiterates that marine VHF equipment must be used strictly in accordance with the ITU Radio Regulations described above.

The guidance also addresses the Automatic Identification System (AIS), clarifying that although AIS is not explicitly referenced in COLREG, it can usefully improve situational awareness for identifying ships, tracking targets, and gathering additional information. It cautions watchkeepers, however, that not all vessels carry AIS (particularly small leisure craft, fishing vessels, warships, and some shore stations), and that AIS may in some circumstances be legitimately switched off at a master's discretion — so officers of the watch should not treat the AIS picture as a complete or fully reliable representation of surrounding traffic. Taken together, the Note positions VHF and AIS as supplementary situational-awareness tools that must be used within, not instead of, the established rules and procedures for safe navigation.

"Securité, Securité, Securité" (French for "safety") is used to announce navigational hazards or important safety information to other vessels in the area. It's a safety broadcast, not a distress call.

Examples of Securité broadcasts: Notifying other vessels of floating debris, a navigational aid that is off-station, or broadcasting urgent marine weather warnings.

The Securité call procedure:

Channel Selection: Choose Channel 16 or an appropriate local channel for navigational warnings.
Transmit: Press the transmit button and clearly and slowly say: "Securité, Securité, Securité".
Identify Vessel: State: "This is [Name of your vessel], [Name of your vessel], [Name of your vessel]".
Nature of Warning: Clearly describe the safety information you are broadcasting. "Attention all stations, this is sailing vessel Alert broadcasting a navigational warning. Unmarked floating log observed in position [Location], drifting [Direction]."
"Over": End your transmission with "Over."
 
Securité broadcasts are often used by the Coast Guard and other official agencies to disseminate important safety information. Listen out for Securité calls, especially if you are in areas known for hazards or during periods of inclement weather.

There is the further danger that even if contact and identification is achieved and no difficulties over the language of communication or message content arise, a course of action might still be chosen that does not comply with the Collision Regulations.  This may lead to the collision it was intended to prevent. 10. I must repeat, in the hope that it will achieve some publicity, what I have said on previous occasions that any attempt to use VHF to agree the manner of passing is fraught with the danger of misunderstanding.  Marine Superintendents would be well advised to prohibit such use of VHF radio and to instruct their officers to comply with the Collision Regulations." 11.  In a case published in 2002 one of two vessels, approaching each other in fog, used the VHF radio to call for a red to red (port to port) passing. The call was acknowledged by the other vessel but unfortunately, due to the command of English on the calling vessel, what the caller intended was a green to green (starboard to starboard) passing. The actions were not effectively monitored by either of the vessels and collision followed. 12. Again in a case published in 2006 one of two vessels, approaching one another to involve a close quarter’s situation, agreed to a starboard to starboard passing arrangement with a person on board another, unidentified ship, but not the approaching vessel. Furthermore, the passing agreement required one of the vessels to make an alteration of course, contrary to the requirements of the applicable Rule in the COLREGS. Had the vessel agreed to a passing arrangement requiring her to manoeuvre in compliance with the COLREGS, the ships would have passed clear, despite the misidentification of ships on the VHF radio. Unfortunately by the time both vessels realised that the ships had turned towards each other the distance between them had further reduced to the extent that the last minute avoiding action taken by both ships was unable to prevent a collision. 13. MGN 324 (M+F) is MCA guidance directed at owners, masters, officers, and pilots of merchant ships, nautical training institutions, and owners/skippers of fishing vessels, yachts, and pleasure craft. It has been reissued and amended several times (the current version is "Amendment 2"), each time in response to continuing marine casualties in which misuse of VHF radio was identified as a contributory factor.

Its central message is that although VHF radio can be a useful aid to avoiding collisions, it must never be allowed to override or substitute for compliance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (COLREG) — in other words, a VHF conversation agreeing on a course of action between two vessels does not override the formal collision-avoidance rules, and over-reliance on VHF negotiation to resolve close-quarters situations has itself been a cause of accidents. The Note reiterates that marine VHF equipment must be used strictly in accordance with the ITU Radio Regulations described above.

The guidance also addresses the Automatic Identification System (AIS), clarifying that although AIS is not explicitly referenced in COLREG, it can usefully improve situational awareness for identifying ships, tracking targets, and gathering additional information. It cautions watchkeepers, however, that not all vessels carry AIS (particularly small leisure craft, fishing vessels, warships, and some shore stations), and that AIS may in some circumstances be legitimately switched off at a master's discretion — so officers of the watch should not treat the AIS picture as a complete or fully reliable representation of surrounding traffic. Taken together, the Note positions VHF and AIS as supplementary situational-awareness tools that must be used within, not instead of, the established rules and procedures for safe navigation.

An imprecise or ambiguously expressed message could have serious consequences. 9.  Valuable time can be wasted whilst mariners on vessels approaching each other try to make contact on VHF radio instead of complying with the Collision Regulations. MGN 324 (M+F) is MCA guidance directed at owners, masters, officers, and pilots of merchant ships, nautical training institutions, and owners/skippers of fishing vessels, yachts, and pleasure craft. It has been reissued and amended several times (the current version is "Amendment 2"), each time in response to continuing marine casualties in which misuse of VHF radio was identified as a contributory factor.

Its central message is that although VHF radio can be a useful aid to avoiding collisions, it must never be allowed to override or substitute for compliance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (COLREG) — in other words, a VHF conversation agreeing on a course of action between two vessels does not override the formal collision-avoidance rules, and over-reliance on VHF negotiation to resolve close-quarters situations has itself been a cause of accidents. The Note reiterates that marine VHF equipment must be used strictly in accordance with the ITU Radio Regulations described above.

The guidance also addresses the Automatic Identification System (AIS), clarifying that although AIS is not explicitly referenced in COLREG, it can usefully improve situational awareness for identifying ships, tracking targets, and gathering additional information. It cautions watchkeepers, however, that not all vessels carry AIS (particularly small leisure craft, fishing vessels, warships, and some shore stations), and that AIS may in some circumstances be legitimately switched off at a master's discretion — so officers of the watch should not treat the AIS picture as a complete or fully reliable representation of surrounding traffic. Taken together, the Note positions VHF and AIS as supplementary situational-awareness tools that must be used within, not instead of, the established rules and procedures for safe navigation.

MGN 641 (M) is the MCA's practical guidance document explaining how shipowners, masters, shipbuilders, and seafarers should interpret and apply the Merchant Shipping (Radiocommunications) (Amendment) Regulations 2021 described above. Rather than creating new legal obligations itself, it is meant to be read alongside the 2021 Regulations to clarify what compliance looks like in practice — and in fact parts of the Note have been given the force of law by the Regulations.

The guidance is structured around eight key topic areas: an introduction to the legal framework; how "recognised satellite service providers" are determined; requirements for radio installation on board; the sources of electrical energy that must be available to power radio equipment (including backup power in case of failure); the performance standards equipment must meet; maintenance requirements to keep radio equipment serviceable; qualifications and duties required of radio personnel on board; and the record-keeping obligations for radio logs.

Because the Regulations incorporate future SOLAS amendments automatically via the ambulatory reference mechanism, the guidance note is periodically reissued or amended (there have been at least one or two amendments since first publication in December 2021) to reflect the latest position and remove ambiguity for those applying the rules day to day.

MGN 324 (M+F) is MCA guidance directed at owners, masters, officers, and pilots of merchant ships, nautical training institutions, and owners/skippers of fishing vessels, yachts, and pleasure craft. It has been reissued and amended several times (the current version is "Amendment 2"), each time in response to continuing marine casualties in which misuse of VHF radio was identified as a contributory factor.

Its central message is that although VHF radio can be a useful aid to avoiding collisions, it must never be allowed to override or substitute for compliance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (COLREG) — in other words, a VHF conversation agreeing on a course of action between two vessels does not override the formal collision-avoidance rules, and over-reliance on VHF negotiation to resolve close-quarters situations has itself been a cause of accidents. The Note reiterates that marine VHF equipment must be used strictly in accordance with the ITU Radio Regulations described above.

The guidance also addresses the Automatic Identification System (AIS), clarifying that although AIS is not explicitly referenced in COLREG, it can usefully improve situational awareness for identifying ships, tracking targets, and gathering additional information. It cautions watchkeepers, however, that not all vessels carry AIS (particularly small leisure craft, fishing vessels, warships, and some shore stations), and that AIS may in some circumstances be legitimately switched off at a master's discretion — so officers of the watch should not treat the AIS picture as a complete or fully reliable representation of surrounding traffic. Taken together, the Note positions VHF and AIS as supplementary situational-awareness tools that must be used within, not instead of, the established rules and procedures for safe navigation.

- Traffic participants must indicate in good time if they wish to deviate from a route.
- During navigation assistance, the traffic controller gives an overview of the current traffic picture, possibly supplemented with calculated, expected situations, such as encounters and passages in (passing) distance and time.
- To convey the position of a moving ship, the position of the bow of the vessel relative to a point ahead in the fairway, or in bearing and distance, is used. For a stationary ship, this is the middle of the track or a radar echo.
- The **passing distance** is the distance that will exist during passing between the adjacent sides of two ships, or between a ship and an obstacle. The passing distance is only reliable provided the ground track remains constant.
- The **ground track** of a ship is its direction of movement relative to true north over the ground.
- The **distance between two vessels** is the measured shortest distance. For head-on traffic this is the bow-to-bow distance; for overtaking traffic this is the bow-to-stern distance.
- The **abeam distance** to a buoy, beacon or obstacle is the distance between the bow of a moving ship and an object, measured perpendicular to the direction of the fairway.
- The **distance to a navigation mark** is the shortest distance to that navigation mark.
- The terms **"opvarend" (upbound)** and **"afvarend" (downbound)** are used east of the Schone Waardin. In English these are "ingoing" and "outgoing".
- In the approach areas and the roadstead area, the terms **"inkomend" (inbound)** and **"uitgaand" (outbound)** are used, in English "inbound" and "outbound".
- To indicate a position before or beyond a certain point, we use **"bovenwaarts" (upstream)** or **"benedenwaarts" (downstream)**. In English these are "above" and "below".
- If the traffic controller must give information about a part of the area not covered by radar and for which no visual information is available, he or she will make this known to the traffic participant requesting the information.
- Position information is always given relative to known reference points. These points are visible, known and can be found on the nautical chart.
- A **bearing** between two known points is the horizontal angle relative to true north and the point being observed. The figures are spoken one by one.
- **Distances** are given to a tenth of a kilometre or a tenth of a nautical mile (also called a "cable"). Where confusion is possible, e.g. between the English numbers fifty and fifteen, the digits are spoken separately.
- Names of buoys and markers must not be translated. They are pronounced as they appear on the nautical chart. For example, W6 is pronounced "Whiskey 6".
- "Buoy transit" (doorwisselen van boeien) refers to two consecutive buoys marking a bend in a channel coming into line relative to the bow of the ship.
- Position reports can be given in two ways: using the along/across method, or via bearing and distance. The traffic controller may supplement this with ground track and ground speed. The intervals between reports depend on the traffic picture, the speeds of vessels, meteorological conditions, nautically critical points, and so on.
- An **along/across position report** comprises, on the one hand, the point to which the ship has progressed along the length of the fairway, and on the other hand, the distance of the ship in the transverse direction, measured to the locally customary reference line — for example the buoy line, the light line, the shore, etc. The transverse distance may also be expressed as 1/3 red, 1/3 green, or mid-channel. If the distance is less than 1/3 of the fairway width, the distance is expressed in metres to the buoy line.
  Measurements are always given relative to the starboard side (SB) of the vessel. If this is not possible because there is no reference, the traffic controller will explicitly state this.
- A **position report via bearing and distance** looks at the position of the forward part of the assisted ship in relation to a known point.
  Here too, the traffic controller may add ground track and ground speed. If the ship is sailing parallel to the reference line, moving away from it, or approaching it, this will be stated.
- If the traffic controller gives position reports (on request) while a ship is coming to anchor, he or she agrees which point the reports will be relative to. Either the planned anchor position is indicated — this may be an anchorage as shown on the chart, or a position chosen by the master or pilot. From the bow, the traffic controller gives information by bearing and distance (B/D) to the anchor position, including speed over ground. As a standard for reporting frequency, the following applies:
  - Distance more than 1500 m: B/D every 500 m
  - Distance 1500 to 500 m: B/D every 200 m
  - Distance 500 to 200 m: B/D every 100 m
  - From 200 m: B/D every 50 m.

For anchor watch purposes, the master or pilot must state the number of nautical miles and/or cables relative to a fixed point, and the number of shackles on deck.

The Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS) is an international system using advanced communications technology designed to enhance ship-to-shore communications and provide automated distress alerting. Compliance is mandatory for SOLAS vessels (large cargo and passenger ships) on international voyages or in open seas. For smaller fishing boats and commercial vessels, the availability of GMDSS equipment is required by the national legislation of maritime countries (with reduced carriage requirements). At present, GMDSS is voluntary for small craft and pleasure boats, but a growing number of vessels are fitted with GMDSS radiocommunications equipment and can take advantage of the benefits of this distress and safety system. The principle of GMDSS is that search-and-rescue authorities ashore, as well as shipping in the immediate vicinity of a ship in distress, will be rapidly alerted to a distress incident so that they can assist in a coordinated Search and Rescue (SAR) operation with the minimum of delay. The system also provides for the promulgation of Maritime Safety Information (MSI), for example navigational and meteorological warnings and forecasts and other urgent safety information to ships. GMDSS ensures in the whole world the totality of the radiocommunications necessary for safeguarding human life at sea. You must therefore carefully consider the options that are available to you, thinking about your own needs for training and equipment in order to understand and use GMDSS.
